title: Pivoting and deduplication
summary: Turn rows into columns and back, and keep one row of each duplicate.

steps.title: Pivot: rows into columns
body: Group finance wants a grid: one row per month, one column per business. The data is *long* (one row per month per business). **Pivot** it with conditional aggregation, the CASE trick from module 2:
```sql
SELECT month,
SUM(CASE WHEN business = 'books'   THEN revenue END) AS books,
SUM(CASE WHEN business = 'bikes'   THEN revenue END) AS bikes,
SUM(CASE WHEN business = 'theatre' THEN revenue END) AS theatre
FROM sales
GROUP BY month;

A missing combination comes out NULL (wrap in `COALESCE(..., 0)` for a zero). SQL Server and Oracle also have a `PIVOT` operator; PostgreSQL has `crosstab` in an extension. The CASE version works everywhere.
The reverse, **unpivot** (columns into rows), is a `UNION ALL` of one SELECT per column.

steps.title: The finance grid
prompt: Return one row per **month** (in order) with columns **books**, **bikes** and **theatre** holding that month's revenue, `0` where there is none.
Tables: `sales(month, business, revenue)` (one row per month per business) and `contacts(id, email, name, city, updated_at)`.
solution: COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN business = 'books' THEN revenue END), 0) AS books,
COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN business = 'bikes' THEN revenue END), 0) AS bikes,
COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN business = 'theatre' THEN revenue END), 0) AS theatre
setup: CREATE TABLE sales (month TEXT, business TEXT, revenue INTEGER, PRIMARY KEY (month, business));
CREATE TABLE contacts (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT, name TEXT, city TEXT, updated_at TEXT);

steps.explain: Each column becomes its own row. `VALUES` in a CTE is a quick way to make a tiny table.

steps.title: Duplicates
body: Ana is in `contacts` three times: she moved city, and once typed her name differently. Which row is the truth? Usually **the latest**. Number each email's rows newest first, then keep number 1:
```sql
WITH ranked AS (
SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS n
FROM contacts
SELECT id, email, name, city FROM ranked WHERE n = 1;
To **delete** the extra rows instead, find the ids to keep and delete the rest:
```sql
DELETE FROM contacts
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM ranked WHERE n = 1);   -- with the CTE in front
Always look before deleting: run the SELECT, then the DELETE in a transaction.

prompt: Return one row per email, the **most recently updated** one: **email**, **name**, **city**.
Tables: `sales(month, business, revenue)` (one row per month per business) and `contacts(id, email, name, city, updated_at)`.
solution: SELECT email, name, city, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS n
SELECT email, name, city FROM ranked WHERE n = 1;

steps.prompt: Arrange the statements to safely remove duplicate contacts, keeping the newest.
lines: WITH ranked AS (SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS n FROM contacts)
DELETE FROM contacts WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM ranked WHERE n > 1);
SELECT email, COUNT(*) FROM contacts GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
steps.explain: Open a transaction, delete everything but the newest per email, check no duplicates remain, then commit.

steps.title: Clean up for real
prompt: Delete the duplicate contacts, keeping only the **most recently updated** row for each email.
Tables: `sales(month, business, revenue)` (one row per month per business) and `contacts(id, email, name, city, updated_at)`.
solution: SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS n
DELETE FROM contacts WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM ranked WHERE n > 1);
